concepts.title: Photosynthetic Pigments and the Light Reaction
concepts.section: 11.2 Early Experiments, 11.3 Pigments, 11.6 The Electron Transport
concepts.definition: Photosynthesis uses pigments arranged in photosystem I and photosystem II; the splitting of water releases oxygen, electrons pass through the Z scheme of electron carriers producing ATP and NADPH in the light reaction, and photophosphorylation may be non-cyclic or cyclic.
concepts.key_idea: The reaction centre of photosystem II is called P680 and of photosystem I is P700, and cyclic photophosphorylation operates in photosystem I alone producing only ATP.
question_patterns: describe the z scheme of light reaction
differentiate photosystem i and photosystem ii
what is photophosphorylation and its two types
why is the splitting of water called photolysis
state the role of pigments like chlorophyll a carotenoids and xanthophylls
where does the light reaction occur in the chloroplast

solution_steps.explain: Place P680 and P700 in the thylakoid membrane.
Follow the Z scheme from water splitting to NADP reduction.
Confirm ATP and NADPH as the products of the light reaction.

concepts.title: Calvin Cycle and the ATP Requirement per Glucose
concepts.section: 11.7 Where are the ATP and NADPH used?
concepts.definition: The Calvin cycle fixes carbon dioxide using ATP and NADPH of the light reaction, and for the formation of one molecule of glucose the cycle requires eighteen ATP and twelve NADPH, fixing six molecules of carbon dioxide in carboxylation steps.
concepts.key_idea: RuBP carboxylation, reduction and regeneration of RuBP are the three stages of the Calvin cycle, and the energy budget of eighteen ATP per glucose shows the cost of carbon fixation.
question_patterns: how many atp are required to make one glucose molecule in the calvin cycle
calculate the atp demand for synthesising a given number of glucose molecules
describe the three stages of the calvin cycle
what is the role of rubisco in carbon fixation
how many nadph are used per glucose in the calvin cycle
why is regeneration of rubp necessary

solution_steps.explain: Multiply the number of glucose molecules by 18 to get the ATP needed in the Calvin cycle

concepts.title: C4 Pathway and Photorespiration
concepts.definition: In C4 plants the Hatch and Slack pathway fixes carbon dioxide in mesophyll cells using PEP carboxylase into oxaloacetic acid, which is transported to bundle sheath cells for the Calvin cycle, avoiding the wasteful photorespiration seen in C3 plants where rubisco oxygenates RuBP.
concepts.key_idea: The Kranz anatomy of bundle sheath cells and the high CO2 affinity of PEP carboxylase make C4 plants like maize and sugarcane more efficient in hot climates.
question_patterns: describe the hatch and slack pathway in c4 plants
what is kranz anatomy and where is it seen
differentiate c3 and c4 plants
why is photorespiration absent in c4 plants
explain the role of pep carboxylase in carbon fixation
why is photorespiration called a wasteful process

solution_steps.explain: Separate mesophyll carboxylation from bundle sheath decarboxylation.
Note the absence of rubisco oxygenation in mesophyll of C4 plants.
Confirm Kranz anatomy supports the pathway.

concepts.title: Factors Affecting Photosynthesis
concepts.definition: Photosynthesis is governed by internal factors such as chlorophyll and leaf age, and external factors of light, carbon dioxide concentration, temperature and water, following Blackman's law of limiting factors.
concepts.key_idea: When several factors affect a process, the rate is decided by the factor nearest its minimal value, which is the law of limiting factors.
question_patterns: state blackman's law of limiting factors
how does light intensity affect the rate of photosynthesis
why does photosynthesis decline at high temperatures
what is the effect of increased carbon dioxide on c3 plants
list the internal and external factors of photosynthesis
explain water stress effect on photosynthesis

solution_steps.explain: Note light, carbon dioxide, temperature, water and chlorophyll.
Identify the factor closest to its minimum that controls the rate.
State how improving the limiting factor changes the rate.
